content: Genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a chronic, recurrent condition with no known cure. The virus is composed of a DNA core, a capsid, a tegument, and an envelope. There are two types of HSV: HSV-1 and HSV-2, which differ in their envelope proteins. HSV-1 is typically associated with orolabial infections, while HSV-2 is more commonly linked to genital infections. However, both types can cause cutaneous infections at other body sites. Genital herpes is a widespread condition, particularly in the United States, where its prevalence has been increasing over recent decades. Risk factors for HSV-2 infection include a higher number of lifetime sexual partners and a history of other sexually transmitted infections. Globally, genital herpes is recognized as a significant sexually transmitted disease, affecting millions of individuals. The seroprevalence of HSV-2 varies widely, ranging from 10% in some Asian countries to as high as 80% in certain sub-Saharan African regions. The infection typically affects adolescents and adults after the initiation of sexual activity, with a peak incidence during middle to late adolescence. Most cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, although HSV-1 is becoming increasingly common in younger adults and women. The condition has a profound impact on patients' quality of life and work productivity. In the United States, it is a major public health issue, contributing to significant healthcare costs due to diagnostic testing, treatment, and medical care. Nearly all patients with HSV-2 experience at least one recurrence after the initial outbreak, with approximately 38% experiencing more than six recurrences annually. The median recurrence rate is four episodes per year. Although recurrences are generally less severe and shorter in duration than the primary outbreak, they can still cause significant physical pain and emotional distress. Patients with genital herpes often experience anxiety about the social implications of their condition, the risk of transmitting the virus to their partners, and the challenge of disclosing their health status to new sexual partners. Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals are particularly vulnerable to severe outcomes. Approximately 22% of pregnant women are seropositive for HSV, and 2% acquire a new infection during pregnancy. Vertical transmission of HSV, particularly during a primary episode in the third trimester, can result in severe morbidity and mortality in neonates if untreated. Immunocompromised patients often experience more severe and atypical disease progression. Additionally, HSV-2 infection increases the risk of HIV acquisition and transmission by creating a susceptible environment in the genital mucosa and increasing the population of HIV target cells. The initial stage of HSV infection begins when the virus enters the body through the skin or mucosa during direct sexual contact with an infected individual. The virus replicates in the epidermis, causing cellular damage and inflammation, before traveling to the peripheral nerves and establishing latency in the nervous system. Clinical symptoms typically appear four to seven days after exposure and can include redness, fluid-filled blisters, and ulcers that eventually crust and heal without scarring. Local symptoms may include pain and tenderness in the affected area, as well as swollen lymph nodes. Systemic symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle pain, and urinary discomfort are also common. Primary infections, particularly in individuals without pre-existing antibodies to HSV, tend to be more severe. During the latent stage, patients are asymptomatic, but viral shedding can still occur, leading to transmission. Reactivations occur when the latent virus migrates to the skin or mucous membranes, causing recurrent outbreaks. These recurrences are generally milder and shorter in duration than the initial infection, with fewer days of viral shedding and lower viral concentrations. Prodromal symptoms, such as altered sensation or pain in the buttocks, thighs, hips, or perineum, may precede the appearance of lesions by 30 minutes to 48 hours. Stress and anxiety are known to increase the risk of recurrences. Compared to HSV-1, HSV-2 is associated with more frequent and severe outbreaks. Diagnosis of genital herpes can be achieved through viral culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing, or type-specific serologic testing (TSST). Viral culture is useful for distinguishing between HSV-1 and HSV-2 but has lower sensitivity during recurrences or the healing phase of an outbreak. PCR testing is faster and more sensitive, particularly during active lesions. TSST detects IgG antibodies specific to HSV-1 or HSV-2 but may yield false-negative results in the early stages of infection. TSST is particularly useful for patients with recurrent or atypical symptoms and negative viral cultures. Treatment for recurrent genital herpes primarily involves nucleoside analogues such as aciclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir. These antiviral drugs inhibit viral DNA replication by incorporating phosphorylated molecules into the viral DNA chain and blocking viral polymerase. Aciclovir is highly effective against HSV-1 and less so against HSV-2. However, its oral bioavailability is low (10-20%), necessitating frequent dosing. Valaciclovir, a prodrug of aciclovir, has significantly higher oral bioavailability (approximately 54%) and requires less frequent dosing. Famciclovir, a prodrug of penciclovir, has even higher bioavailability (77%) and achieves higher intracellular concentrations due to its affinity for thymidine kinase. All three drugs are primarily excreted by the kidneys, and caution is advised in patients with renal dysfunction. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, and diarrhea, while serious adverse events are rare. Resistance to nucleoside analogues is primarily due to mutations in viral enzymes involved in drug activation and is more common in immunocompromised patients. Episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes involves short courses of antiviral treatment during outbreaks, typically lasting two to five days. This approach is most effective when initiated during the prodromal phase, before lesions appear. Patients are educated to recognize prodromal symptoms and begin treatment promptly. Episodic therapy is generally recommended for patients with mild and infrequent recurrences. Compared to suppressive therapy, which involves daily antiviral treatment over several months, episodic therapy may result in fewer side effects and lower costs. However, evidence regarding the effectiveness of episodic therapy in reducing symptoms and viral replication is limited. Further research, including systematic reviews, is needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes.
